Content:
There is some nice intuition behind Green's theorem that makes it easier to remember.

Content:
Suppose that [MATH: \mathbf F] is a vector field on [MATH: \mathbb R^2] with domain [MATH: D] and component functions [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q.] So, we have
[MATH: \mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j.]

Content:
Green's theorem states that the sum of the microscopic curls of [MATH: \mathbf F] inside [MATH: D] equals the macroscopic curl of [MATH: \mathbf F] at the boundary of [MATH: D.]

Content:
To keep the picture simple, we will deliberately choose [MATH: D] to be a rectangle and imagine breaking it into many tiny squares.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6f11bff33e18a32f02e6a6d1eb18979e]

Content:
Here is the key idea.

Content:
- Each tiny square has its own local circulation, which is measured by the scalar curl
[MATH: \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}.]
If we sum (integrate) the curl at every point over the entire domain [MATH: D,] we get
[MATH: \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\mathrm{d}A.]
- On the other hand, when we add up the contributions from all the tiny squares, the integrals along shared interior edges cancel:

- one square traverses a shared edge in one direction,
- the neighboring square traverses the same edge in the opposite direction.
- Because of this cancellation, the only edges that do not get canceled are the edges on the outer boundary [MATH: C.]

Content:
So, when we “sum all the microscopic curls” across [MATH: D,] what remains is exactly the “macroscopic curl,” meaning the circulation around the boundary:
[MATH: \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\mathrm{d}A
=
\oint\limits_{C}\mathbf F\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf r]

Content:
Finally, using [MATH: \mathbf F(x,y)=P(x,y)\,\mathbf i+Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j,] we can write the circulation as a line integral with respect to [MATH: x] and [MATH: y{:}]
[MATH: \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\mathrm{d}A
=
\oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y]

Content:
Let's now look at a concrete example of how to apply Green's theorem.

Graphic:

Content:
We will use Green's theorem, which states that

Content:

Content:
We denote [MATH: P(x,y)= xy^2] and [MATH: Q(x,y)= 2x^2y.] Then, we have

Content:
[MATH: (∂P)/(∂y) = 2xy, (∂Q)/(∂x) = 4xy.]

Content:
Applying Green's theorem, we obtain

Content:
[MATH: ∮_(C)xy^{2}dx + 2x^{2}ydy|= ∬_(D)((∂Q)/(∂x) − (∂P)/(∂y))dA; = ∬_(D)(4xy − 2xy)dA; = ∫_{0}^{1}∫_{0}^{2x}2xydydx.]

Content:
Calculating this repeated integral using the usual methods, we obtain

Content:
[MATH: \int_0^1 \int _0^{2x} 2xy \,\textrm d{y} \: \textrm{d}x = 1.]

Content:
Therefore, we conclude that

Content:
[MATH: \oint\limits_{C} xy^2 \: \mathrm{d}x+ 2x^2y \: \mathrm{d}y = 1.]

Content:
This example demonstrates the power of Green's theorem. Direct evaluation of the line integral involves splitting [MATH: C] into three separate paths and evaluating each separately. With Green's theorem, we reduced the entire problem to a single, relatively straightforward double integral.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose that [MATH: f(x)] is continuous on [MATH: [a,b].] The fundamental theorem of calculus states that

Content:
[MATH: \int_a^b f'(x)\,\textrm d x = f(b) - f(a).]

Content:
This theorem relates the integral of [MATH: f'] over the domain [MATH: D = [a,b]] to the values of [MATH: f] at the boundary of [MATH: D.] Here, the boundary of [MATH: D] consists of the endpoints [MATH: x=a] and [MATH: x=b] only.

Content:
An analogous result, known as Green's theorem, exists for double integrals. It states the following:

Content:
> Let [MATH: C] be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, and simple closed curve in [MATH: \Bbb R^2,] and let [MATH: D] be the region enclosed by [MATH: C.] If [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] are scalar functions that have continuous partial derivatives, then
> [MATH: \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right) \: \textrm{d}A = \oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y.]

Content:
Green's theorem is seen as an analog of the fundamental theorem of calculus because it relates an integral of the derivatives of [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] over a domain [MATH: D] to the values of [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] on the boundary of [MATH: D.]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Intuition Behind Green's Theorem

Content:
There is some nice intuition behind Green's theorem that makes it easier to remember.

Content:
Suppose that [MATH: \mathbf F] is a vector field on [MATH: \mathbb R^2] with domain [MATH: D] and component functions [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q.] So, we have
[MATH: \mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j.]

Content:
Green's theorem states that the sum of the microscopic curls of [MATH: \mathbf F] inside [MATH: D] equals the macroscopic curl of [MATH: \mathbf F] at the boundary of [MATH: D.]

Content:
To keep the picture simple, we will deliberately choose [MATH: D] to be a rectangle and imagine breaking it into many tiny squares.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6f11bff33e18a32f02e6a6d1eb18979e]

Content:
Here is the key idea.

Content:
- Each tiny square has its own local circulation, which is measured by the scalar curl
[MATH: \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}.]
If we sum (integrate) the curl at every point over the entire domain [MATH: D,] we get
[MATH: \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\mathrm{d}A.]
- On the other hand, when we add up the contributions from all the tiny squares, the integrals along shared interior edges cancel:

- one square traverses a shared edge in one direction,
- the neighboring square traverses the same edge in the opposite direction.
- Because of this cancellation, the only edges that do not get canceled are the edges on the outer boundary [MATH: C.]

Content:
So, when we “sum all the microscopic curls” across [MATH: D,] what remains is exactly the “macroscopic curl,” meaning the circulation around the boundary:
[MATH: \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\mathrm{d}A
=
\oint\limits_{C}\mathbf F\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf r]

Content:
Finally, using [MATH: \mathbf F(x,y)=P(x,y)\,\mathbf i+Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j,] we can write the circulation as a line integral with respect to [MATH: x] and [MATH: y{:}]
[MATH: \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\mathrm{d}A
=
\oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y]

Content:
Let's now look at a concrete example of how to apply Green's theorem.

Item 3 — Tutorial: A Concrete Example

Content:
Suppose we wish to compute the line integral

Content:
[MATH: \oint\limits_{C} xy^2 \: \mathrm{d}x+ 2x^2y \: \mathrm{d}y]

Content:
where [MATH: C] is the boundary of the region [MATH: D,] given by

Content:
[MATH: D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq y \leq 2x \big\}.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ed956fb1e8c79b09478a079dc335e9a1]

Content:
We will use Green's theorem, which states that

Content:
[MATH: \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right) \: \textrm{d}A = \oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y.]

Content:
We denote [MATH: P(x,y)= xy^2] and [MATH: Q(x,y)= 2x^2y.] Then, we have

Content:
[MATH: (∂P)/(∂y) = 2xy, (∂Q)/(∂x) = 4xy.]

Content:
Applying Green's theorem, we obtain

Content:
[MATH: ∮_(C)xy^{2}dx + 2x^{2}ydy|= ∬_(D)((∂Q)/(∂x) − (∂P)/(∂y))dA; = ∬_(D)(4xy − 2xy)dA; = ∫_{0}^{1}∫_{0}^{2x}2xydydx.]

Content:
Calculating this repeated integral using the usual methods, we obtain

Content:
[MATH: \int_0^1 \int _0^{2x} 2xy \,\textrm d{y} \: \textrm{d}x = 1.]

Content:
Therefore, we conclude that

Content:
[MATH: \oint\limits_{C} xy^2 \: \mathrm{d}x+ 2x^2y \: \mathrm{d}y = 1.]

Content:
This example demonstrates the power of Green's theorem. Direct evaluation of the line integral involves splitting [MATH: C] into three separate paths and evaluating each separately. With Green's theorem, we reduced the entire problem to a single, relatively straightforward double integral.

Item 13 — Tutorial: Green's Theorem in Vector Form

Content:
It's possible to write Green's theorem in a form that explicitly features the curl.

Content:
To demonstrate, let's denote [MATH: \mathbf{F}(x,y) = \big\langle P(x,y), \: Q(x,y) \big\rangle.] According to Green's theorem,

Content:
[MATH: \oint\limits_C \mathbf{F}(x,y) \cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}
= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\textrm d A.]

Content:
Now, by thinking of [MATH: \mathbf{F}] as a vector field on [MATH: \mathbb R^3] with zero [MATH: z]-component, we can write
[MATH: \mathbf{F}(x,y,0) = \big\langle P(x,y), \: Q(x,y), \: 0 \big\rangle.]

Content:
Computing the curl of [MATH: \mathbf F(x,y,0),] we obtain

Content:
[MATH: i|j|k; (∂)/(∂x)|(∂)/(∂y)|(∂)/(∂z); P|Q|0]

Content:
As a result, we can recover the original scalar curl by taking the dot product of [MATH: \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F] with the vector [MATH: \mathbf k\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \text{curl}\:\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{k} = \left(\dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial y}\right) \mathbf k \cdot \mathbf k = \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial y}]

Content:
Therefore, we can write Green's theorem in the form

Content:
[MATH: \oint\limits_C \mathbf{F}(x,y) \cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}
= \iint\limits_D {\text{curl}\:\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{k}} \, \textrm d A.]
